newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Tapie admits illicit soccer "loans".
newsitem.headline: France's Tapie admits illicit soccer "loans".

text.p: Fallen French soccer tycoon Bernard Tapie admitted in court on Wednesday breaking the law with fictitious loans to star players of his former European champions Marseille which turned out to be tax-free payments.
Under questioning about a one-million franc ($170,000) "loan" to French World Cup star Alain Giresse, Tapie said the club chose a tax arrangement which "was illicit, but less than others".

Giresse "was in a serious situation, he needed one million cash," he added on the third day of his trial, with other former club officials, over the disappearance of 100 million francs ($17 million) from Marseille accounts.

The investigating magistrate has singled out two other such loans -- of eight million francs ($1.4 million) to Karl-Heinz Foerster in 1986 and three million francs ($510,000) to Philippe Vercruysse in 1988.

Tapie, a 54-year-old bankrupt tycoon and former cabinet minister, is serving an eight-month jail sentence for rigging a soccer match in 1993. He faces a five-year sentence if convicted on charges of swindling, misusing corporate funds and falsifying documents.
His former right-hand man Jean-Pierre Bernes, who has turned into his worst enemy since the match-rigging trial, described the loans as compensation rather than bonuses in disguise.
"Players got tax-free sums when they joined, and Marseille did not have to pay payroll taxes. It was better to pay players by loans rather than run a clandestine fund," he said.
Presiding judge Pierre Richarde said describing the payments as loans was a falsification as they were disguised bonuses.
Co-defendant Alain Laroche, Marseille's former finance director, said he had voiced surprise at the "loans" when he joined Marseille but was told it was normal practice.
He said the system was more widely used by other French clubs than by Marseille although he knew of two other loans, to players Jean-Pierre Papin and Gerard Banide.
Lawyers expressed surprise that the players who benefitted from the loans were not on trial or at least called as witnesses. Richarde admitted they could have been prosecuted.
Other co-defendants passed the buck. Michel Hidalgo, a former Marseille sporting director and French national soccer coach, said he signed the loans on management orders.
"My business is the pitch. On loans, I am zero," he said.

The trial, expected to last three weeks, could shed light on alleged soccer corruption after Bernes promised "revelations". He has accused Tapie of spending five to six million francs ($850,000 to $1 million) a year on rigging French league and European cup games.
